messages.subject: Detection probability greater than 1
parts:
I am using R's Distance package to analyse distance sampling data I collected this past summer. No detection function (the line in the graph below) is fitting my data. I think it's because the detection probability (the bar below) is greater than 1 at distance 0. Why might this be? Do I need more complicated detection functions or could there a problem with my data? See code, graph, and start of my data below.

butter=read.csv("distance sampling 2018_whole prairie_R.csv")

butter.trunc=5 #truncate distance to 5 m

cobutter.hn=ds(butter,truncation=butter.trunc, 
             key="hn",adjustment=NULL,formula=~prop)
plot(cobutter.hn)

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Detection probability greater than 1
parts:
Hello Rachel

Don't interpret the bars of the combined detection function/data histogram figure as a probability; that definition applies to the curve, not the bars.  You don't say if these are line or point transects; the default for the ds() function is line transects, so I'll work on that assumption.  You also do not mention your species, but I'm guessing that because they fly and because your data are truncated at 5 metres, they might be insects.

Now about the lack of fit.  Indeed, your data are unlikely to fit the half normal function depicted there.  However, you'll likely need to look more finely at the histogram (rather than cutpoints at 0.5, you might want cutpoints at 0.1 units for the first 0.5, then 0.25 between 0.5 and 1.5, ...)  This will give you a better appreciation for the shape of your histogram.

However, I note from your 9 detection data provided that the resolution of the measurements seem to be 0.5 units--so a finer histogram might not tell you much more than the histogram you already have.  Snooping further into your data I see "behaviour" of flying/sitting; and that 8 of the 9 detections are with behaviour=flying.  One interpretation of this is that your objects are moving (flying) for the most part and that you (observer=RB) watch them and as they fly they eventually cross the transect, and you record a distance of 0.  That leads to a preponderance of 0's in your data, and you end up with the data you show with a spike in the first histogram bin.  As you note, data such as these are very difficult to fit.

You might want to consult section 10.6 of Buckland et al. (2015) where there is a short section of analysis of butterfly data.   Hope that is of some use to you.

messages.author: 9dce01a6123da978
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Detection probability greater than 1
parts:
Hi Rachael,

Two other situations that could give rise to a detection probability like this is if:
1. detection probability varies with habitat or detection method, and this in turn varies with distance. For example, if you are surveying butterflies in tall grasses, you might disturb the ones straight in front of you (accounting for their much greater visibility) but the ones immediately to the side might stay put and so you would only see a few of them. Similar to Eric's observation, but this issue would still apply even if you recorded butterflies as you are supposed to (i.e. where you first detect them). The distance assumption that is being transgressed here is, I think, that the observer doesn't affect the behaviour or distribution of the study subject.
2. the butterflies themselves might be non-uniformly distributed so that there are more along your line than in the rest of the habitat. For example, if you were walking along a narrow earthen path, many butterflies might be sunning themselves on it. Most of your observations seem to be flying, as Eric pointed out, but perhaps you record them in the mode of behaviour that you first spot them, and you didn't see them before they flew? If so then you should probably be recording the mode of behaviour that you can infer was happening before the butterfly detected you (so that the assumption that what you are recording isn't influenced by your own actions can hold). However, the non-uniform distribution of butterflies on the path could be a more intractable problem, I think.

Cheers,

Mark
